title: The two-language grocery list: six items your child finds in the store
description: Write this week's grocery list together in two languages on any scrap of paper, then let your child find six of the items in the store. An errand you already run, turned into vocabulary.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: The two-language grocery list: six items your child finds in the store
body:
You are going to the store anyway. The list you write before you go can do double work.

At home, take any scrap of paper — the back of an envelope is fine — and pick six items from this week's shopping that your child can recognise: milk, bread, eggs, apples, cheese, carrots. Write each one in both languages, the language you are building first. If Spanish is the one you are building: "la leche — milk". If it is English: "milk — la leche". Your child adds a small drawing next to each word; the drawing is what they will actually read in the store.

Read the list together once before leaving. That is the only "study" part.

In the store, the list belongs to your child. At each aisle, ask for the next item in the language you are building: "¿Dónde está el pan?" — or "where is the bread?". They find it, say the word, and cross it off. Crossing off is the reward; nothing else is needed.

If they point without saying the word, say it for them and move on. The point is to hear and use each word while the object is in their hands, not to pass a checkpoint at every shelf.

Back home, unpacking is round two. Take items out of the bag one at a time and let your child name them: "¡los huevos!" or "the eggs!". Then stick the list on the fridge until next week's shop.

Next week, keep three items and add three new ones. Food works well because it comes back every week — oranges, rice, tomatoes: las naranjas, el arroz, los tomates.

Two small things. Keep the article with each Spanish noun (el pan, la leche, los huevos, las manzanas, el queso, las zanahorias) so it becomes part of the word. And stay at six items even if your child wants more: a list they can finish is better than one they give up on halfway down the aisle.

A busy store is not the place for anything longer. If the trip is rushed, let your child hold the list and simply tick things off while you name them. They still hear every word, in the place where it belongs.
qa_checklist: A bilingual (EN/ES) reader checks both languages, not a tool
No claims about fluency, test scores or developmental outcomes
Every activity works with what is already in the house: no printer, no purchase
Original text written for this page, not lifted from the book
CTA is honest: a Kindle vocabulary book read on a screen, lists copied into a notebook
semantic_review: English body; Spanish food nouns with articles, all neutral (no words for banana, potato or yogurt, which vary). Question script in both directions. List order flips with the language being built.
claims_check: No outcome promises. The text says what to do and how long it takes; it does not claim fluency, school results or cognitive benefits.

checks_run: direction symmetry (either language may be the target)
resolved: examples run in both directions and the instructions name 'the language you are building'
Spanish kept to short words and phrases with articles and accents checked
closing mention of the book cut to one sentence after the activity is fully explained
dropped food words with strong regional variants (banana, potato, yogurt)
added the opening ¡ to the Spanish exclamation
closing sentence about the book removed: the CTA lives on the book card (CLAUDE.md, 12 Sep round four)
